topComments.author: ninkendo
topComments.text: Constructors are such an odd duck to me. On the one hand, you have languages like C++ and Swift which have construction as a first-class concept, with tons of rules you need to memorize (Swift's "convenience" vs "designated" initializers are a real treat to unpack). Then you have languages like Rust, Go, Zig, etc which don't have them at all, constructors are just static functions in the namespace of the type, which return an instance of that type. For the life of me I've never understood why you'd want the former. I'm sure there's a reason, but I never miss it when using languages in the latter category. The explanation you typically hear is about OO and inheritance, but I don't buy it: If Animal had a ::new() that initialized private state, Cow could have a ::new() too that could call Animal::new() if it wanted, then do further initialization, etc... I don't think there's anything about inheritance that says constructors are a must. (Edit: In fact, ObjC does exactly this. I should have remembered that given that I did ObjC for a living for a while.)

topComments.author: spacechild1
topComments.text: The example is pretty contrived because in practice you'd want to zero-initialize the members in the default constructor anyway. struct span { const char *p = nullptr; size_t len = 0; span() = default; // or span() {} span(const char *s, size_t n) : p(s), len(n) {} }; In that case, there is no difference between span s; and span s{}; There are only few use cases where you want a default constructor that does not initialize its members. One example are wrappers around primitive types where you want to closely preserve the original semantics. Whether that's a good idea in the first place really depends on the use case. For example, std::atomic used to default-initialize the underlying value, which led to many bugs in user code. Since C++20 std::atomic uses value-initialization. See https://cplusplus.github.io/LWG/issue2334 . On the one hand, std::atomic is now safer to use, on the other hand, it is not an implicit-lifetime-type anymore, which means you can't put it in shared memory without UB... Another example is glm::vec, which has actually hit me a few times in my own code. At least they recognized the issue and allowed to override the default behavior with the GLM_FORCE_CTOR_INIT define.

stories.title: Show HN: Rchive – Every drive I've owned since the 90s, searchable in one window
stories.author: kevinsync

topComments.author: kevinsync
topComments.text: I posted this and went to bed, and now figure I probably ought to at least write up some of the actual tech, implementation and features, and there's so much that I don't even know where to begin lol. RCHIVE does indeed use Electron. I know that's probably going to catch a lot of flak, but I chose it intentionally due to things I wanted to do in the UI that, hate to say it, Chromium does out of the box that would become a whole sidequest trying to do in Qt or Swift. The front end is underpinned by a variety of daemons and services written in Rust that handle scan coordination and watching, shared platform primitives, executing copy jobs, handling offline geography, decoding media (using OS-native decoders and handling legacy formats), etc. There are other coordinators and workers in Node as well. Database is SQLite, which manages your catalog and executes searches via regular indexes and FTS5 trigram indexes. There's a whole gang of stuff in there to optimize and facilitate searches based on filename/path substrings, scanned metadata, etc. Will be releasing an update with indexing and searching of actual file contents soon. Different people will use RCHIVE for different purposes: - Search/Find: you can see the most recently-changed files, deep-search across all sources, filter based on a bunch of different parameters, etc. You can get just a list of results, or see everything hierarchically in File Browser. Every file that can generate a preview gets one, and there's contextual clustering that happens where appropriate (ex. RCHIVE looks for evidence in sibling files to make decisions based on consensus, such as "folder with 20 MP3s all tagged appropriately, and a couple stray JPGs of unknown provenance -- these very likely all belong together"). Filters are combinatorial and have their own structured syntax, so you can type them out if you want, or use the UI. Previews show images, animated video frames, rendered PDF pages, etc, so you can zip through a bunch of IMG_0XXX files super fast. There's also a "Mini Mode" that's just a search box, so you can start the app, minimize to system tray, then hotkey to search from any other app. Ctrl-shift-R, type, enter, keyboard search, enter to open. Just as easy as Spotlight et al. - Organize: you can take a massive, disparate catalog and apply Recipes (to filter/reduce the dataset) and Transformations (to group and restructure the file tree) to virtually build an organized filesystem, which you can then simply browse, or copy/move some-or-all of it from its messy origin to a tidy destination (new drive, NAS, whatever) -- both recipes and transformations are JSON, so while RCHIVE ships with a ton of presets, you can write your own to basically do whatever you want. The recipe engine is composible and honestly really neat, because you can end up crafting really specific, reusable combination views of all your shit (which then stay updated if you manually rescan, or turn background scanning on). Tagging is also very comprehensive; descendants inherit them by default, but can disinherit granularly. Makes it really easy to tag large swaths of things from a parent - Copy/Move: granular jobs get created which then are executed via rchive-runner (either on CLI or in-app) -- every individual filesystem action is tracked and able to resume/rerun, so if you're copying 10TB of stuff, your power can go out and you don't have to start over. You can pause and come back days later. Care is taken to ensure that stuff like a file "move" isn't marked complete and source isn't removed until file is copied and verified at the destination (either simple verification, or full SHA256 hash checks if needed) There's all kinds of other random useful stuff in there: - all geo/location functions use H3, GeoNames data, and some custom projections and custom data, all offline/on-device. I handle Earth like a truncated icosahedron at varying levels of resolutions, and it rips through locations by bucketing everything into 3D hexagonal tiles which makes lookups easy and fast - you can take a photo of each source for quick identification (ex. "that yellow thumb drive") -- you just click the source, scan a QR code that pops up with your phone, take the photo with your phone, submit - you can "cold copy" paths/drives without cataloging them, like if you simply want to run a job from point A to B - there's pretty comprehensive keyboard support, complex selections, undo/redo, etc - you can make complex selections and then "isolate" the selection, so you're only working with a chosen subset of your catalog - when scanning files, we also look for duplicates, files that are "broken" (a JPG that's actually MP3 data), etc -- for instance, I had a drive from 2002 that I guess had some bad sectors, and I copied it off back then and have carried it ever since. I didn't realize a few of the photos "copied" but the drive head actually read from another area that had some music files, and only found out when they got surfaced during an RCHIVE scan 24 years later. Long story short, Winamp plays those JPGs just fine lol - I also integrated PairDrop into it, so you can pretty easily fire off files or selections of files from inside the app directly to your phone or other devices Anyways, that's just a bit more background about what it all is. Happy to discuss further if anybody has any thoughts or questions!

Replacing the placeholders with actual values works, so the query logic itself is correct. The issue is suspected to be related to how the JDBC driver handles parameter types, In the orginal Oracle query, TRUNC(?) implicitly converted the parameter to a date/timestamp. In KingbaseES, data_trunc('day', ?) seems to fail because the JDBC driver sends the parameter as an unknown or varchar type, and database cannot resolve the correct data_trunc overlodad. infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure)
infoqArticles.description: Laura Savino discusses the psychological friction of AI adoption for senior engineers & architects. She explains how shifting from static expertise to learning in public lowers anxiety, accelerates tooling fluency, and prevents burnout. Leaders will discover actionable strategies to support their teams, debunk tech zealotry, and foster an adaptive engineering culture that thrives during upheaval.
infoqArticles.author: Laura Savino

infoqArticles.title: Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts
infoqArticles.description: Rust 1.100.0, released 12 November 2026, stabilises the never type (!) after ten years of work and makes Infallible an alias for it. The release also stabilises the core of the allocator API, adds DropGuard, and gives Cargo an opt-in dependency cooldown setting. Some critics note the allocator design still lacks inline storage support. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15
infoqArticles.description: AWS has raised the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes in all commercial regions, with no opt-in and no new pricing. The limit had stood since 2018. AWS's post lists the costs: twice the concurrency at the same request rate, three-hour SQS visibility timeouts, and Kafka mappings that must be recreated. Practitioners welcome it and ask what belongs elsewhere. B
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Automating Spark Upgrades with Codex Agents at OpenAI
infoqArticles.description: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, Engineering Manager for Data Infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks. By Robert Krzaczyński
infoqArticles.author: Robert Krzaczyński

infoqArticles.title: CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve
infoqArticles.description: New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required. By Craig Risi
infoqArticles.author: Craig Risi

infoqArticles.title: OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando
infoqArticles.description: OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches. By Eran Stiller
infoqArticles.author: Eran Stiller

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Inferencing for Enterprises
infoqArticles.description: Dio Rettori discusses the operational realities of enterprise AI inference. Moving beyond fast token generation, he explores why inference requires dedicated systems engineering, tackles GPU utilization pitfalls, compares on-prem versus cloud TCO, and analyzes multi-agent latency determinism. He shares why teams must embed domain ontology directly into models rather than relying solely on RAG. By
infoqArticles.author: Dio Rettori

infoqArticles.title: Article: Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports
infoqArticles.description: Moving GenAI into high-stakes production requires treating non-determinism as an engineering problem. This architectural blueprint shows engineering leaders and architects how to build trustworthy agentic workflows using knowledge graphs, dual-layer eval judges, CI/CD release gates, and regression testing against golden datasets to automate drafting while maintaining zero-hallucination compliance.
infoqArticles.author: Ritesh Modi, Sasidhar Gudala

infoqArticles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
infoqArticles.description: At QCon San Francisco 2026, OpenAI's Brian Yang described building the ChatGPT ads product with Codex agents and no human-written code. He outlined layered testing, sandboxes, and batched pull request reviews, and noted failure modes such as code "slop" and unsafe agent actions. He advised gradual adoption and framed engineers as managers of agents. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production
infoqArticles.description: At QCon San Francisco, Google's Amanda Walker framed AI agents as an insider-risk problem operating at machine speed, and described identity, credential and containment patterns for running them safely in production. By Mark Silvester
infoqArticles.author: Mark Silvester

infoqArticles.title: How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures
infoqArticles.description: To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone
